name: Warsaw
info: Warsaw is a city on the Vistula in east-central Poland, founded about 1300 by Prince Bolesław II of Masovia, the capital of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth from 1596 and of Poland since 1918.

facts.founded: The Prince of Płock, Bolesław II of Masovia, established the city in about 1300 on the site of a small fishing village called Warszowa; the first document attesting a castellany there dates to 1313.
facts.where: On both banks of the Vistula in the Masovian Plain in east-central Poland, about 260 km from the Baltic Sea and 523 km east of Berlin.
facts.known: Seat of the Dukes of Masovia; capital of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth from 1596; the Warsaw Confederation of 1573; the Constitution of 3 May 1791; the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943 and the Warsaw Uprising of 1944; the rebuilt Old Town
facts.today: Warsaw is the capital and most populous city of Poland and the capital of the Masovian Voivodeship, with about 1.87 million residents.

t: Warsaw grew from a fishing village into the seat of the Dukes of Masovia, and became the capital of the Polish Crown and the Commonwealth when Sigismund III moved his court from Kraków in 1596.
After the partitions it was held by Prussia, ruled as the Duchy of Warsaw and Congress Poland, and then by Russia, until it became the capital of independent Poland on 11 November 1918.
In the Second World War its Jewish population was confined in a ghetto and two uprisings were crushed, and about 85% of the city was destroyed; the Old Town was rebuilt after the war.
dyk: In 1647 Valerianus Magnus performed a vacuum experiment in Warsaw, repeating Torricelli's, which contradicted official European science.

sections.origins:
Warsaw lies on the Vistula in the Masovian Plain, where the river divides the city into a left and a right bank. On the left bank the edge of the moraine plateau, the Warsaw Escarpment, rises 20 to 25 metres in the Old Town and the central district. The first fortified settlements on the site were Bródno, dated to the 9th or 10th century, and Jazdów, dated to the 12th or 13th century. Bródno was burned about 1040 during the uprising of Miecław, one of the Mazovian princes, and Jazdów was raided by Lithuanians in 1262 and by Prince Bolesław II of Masovia in 1281.

A new settlement then rose on the site of a small fishing village called Warszowa, about 3.5 kilometres north of Jazdów. The Prince of Płock, Bolesław II of Masovia, established the city in about 1300, and his brother and successor Konrad II built a wooden castle that the Lithuanians burned. The first document attesting a castellany dates to 1313. The meaning of the name is uncertain. One hypothesis derives it from Warsz, a short form of the name Warcisław, and a folk etymology tells of the fisherman Wars and the mermaid Sawa, who lived in the Vistula.
sections.growth:
In the 14th century the economy rested on crafts and trade, and about 4,500 people lived in the town. The completion of St John's Cathedral in 1390 made Warsaw one of the seats of the Dukes of Masovia, and in 1413 it became the capital of the duchy. In the 15th century a New Town grew beyond the northern wall of the old settlement, each with its own charter and government. Masovia was incorporated into the Polish Crown in 1526, and the population rose to about 20,000, from about 4,500 a century earlier.

Warsaw first became the seat of the General Sejm in 1529 and held it permanently from 1569. In 1596 Sigismund III Vasa moved his court from Kraków, because of the city's central position between Kraków and Vilnius, and by then it had about 14,000 inhabitants. Private districts called jurydyka grew up around the town, owned by nobles and ruled by their own laws. The reigns of the Saxon kings and Stanisław August Poniatowski were a time of great development, and the city had 24,000 inhabitants in 1754 and 115,000 in 1792. The Saxon Garden opened in 1727, the Załuski Library, the first Polish public library, was founded in 1747, and the Commission of National Education was set up in 1773. The census of 1897 recorded 626,000 people, which made Warsaw the third-largest city of the Russian Empire.
sections.rulers:
Warsaw was a seat of the Dukes of Masovia and their capital from 1413. When the last ducal line died out in 1526 the duchy was incorporated into the Polish Crown; it was said that Bona Sforza had the last duke, Janusz III, poisoned. From 1596 it was the capital of the Commonwealth and the Crown. Sigismund III lived in the royal castle for good from 1611. Kings were elected near the city, and in 1704 the gentry dethroned Augustus II at Wielka Wola and elected Stanisław Leszczyński.

The third partition of 1795 gave Warsaw to Prussia, which made it the capital of South Prussia. Napoleon's army liberated it in 1806 and it became the capital of the Duchy of Warsaw. The Congress of Vienna of 1815 gave it to Congress Poland, a constitutional monarchy in personal union with Russia, and after the November Uprising the Russian emperor set up a military administration. German forces entered Warsaw in the summer of 1915, and the Germans left in November 1918. Józef Piłsudski returned on 10 November, and on 11 November 1918 the Regency Council gave him military authority, a date celebrated as the beginning of Poland's independence. In the Second World War the city came under the General Government, a German colonial administration, and in 1945 it became the capital of the Polish People's Republic.
sections.life:
Warsaw was a city of many peoples and faiths. In the 17th century Armenians, Scots and Italians settled there, and in 1691 the Scottish immigrant Alexander Chalmers was elected mayor of the Old Town. The Jews, who were not allowed to settle in the Old Town in the 15th century, lived in the New Town and later in Muranów. In 1573 the city gave its name to the Warsaw Confederation, which established religious freedom in the Commonwealth. The census of 1901 counted 711,988 inhabitants, of whom 56.2% were Catholics, 35.7% Jews, 5% Greek Orthodox Christians and 2.8% Protestants. In the late 1930s the Jews made up about 30% of the city, the second-largest Jewish population in the world after New York.

The city also became a place of learning. Stanisław Konarski founded the Collegium Nobilium in 1740, the predecessor of the University of Warsaw, which was established in 1816. In 1773 the Commission of National Education came into existence. In the 19th century Mayor Sokrates Starynkiewicz had the first water and sewer systems built by the English engineer William Lindley and his son. Between 1850 and 1882 industrialisation raised the population by 134% to 383,000, and the western district of Wola changed from farms and windmills into a centre of factories.
sections.crises:
Warsaw suffered fires, plagues and sieges. In 1515 a fire burned a large part of the Old Town. Between 1655 and 1658 the city was besieged three times and taken and plundered three times by Swedish, Brandenburgian and Transylvanian forces, and Swedish troops took many books and works of art. In the Great Northern War Swedish troops besieged it in 1702, and plague struck in 1708 and a flood in 1713. After the Warsaw Uprising of April 1794 the Russians reached the eastern outskirts on 3 November and stormed Praga, and many of its inhabitants were murdered; up to 20,000 people are estimated to have been killed. Russian troops fired on a crowd on 27 February 1861 and killed five people.

In September 1939 about 31,000 people died in the siege and the bombing, and 10% of the buildings were destroyed. From October 1940 the Germans confined the Jewish population, about 500,000 people, in a ghetto of about 2.6 square kilometres, where many died of hunger and executions. After the Ghetto Uprising of April 1943 the ghetto was destroyed so completely that not even house walls remained. The Warsaw Uprising began on 1 August 1944 and lasted 63 days. Civilian deaths are estimated at 150,000 to 200,000, and the civilians were expelled. Hitler ordered the city razed, and about 85% of it was destroyed. About 700,000 people died in Warsaw during the occupation, and the population fell from about 1,300,000 in 1939 to 420,000 in 1945.
sections.legacy:
The Old Town and the Royal Route were rebuilt in 1953 as they had looked before the war, aided by pictures by many artists, among them Canaletto, and UNESCO inscribed the Old Town on its World Heritage list in 1980. The Royal Castle was rebuilt between 1971 and 1974. The Palace of Culture and Science, finished in 1955, was a gift from the Soviet Union, and the city also built large prefabricated housing estates. In 1951 the area of the city grew from 118 to 411 square kilometres.

The Constitution of 3 May 1791, passed by the Great Sejm in Warsaw, was called by Norman Davies the first constitution of its kind in Europe. The city is also remembered for the Warsaw Confederation of 1573. Its monuments include Sigismund's Column of 1644, the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes and the statue of the Little Insurrectionist. The Mass that John Paul II celebrated in Victory Square in 1979 was understood by many as encouragement for change, and the Round Table talks of 1989 were held in Warsaw. Poland entered the European Union in 2004. Warsaw is today the capital of Poland, with an official population estimate of about 1.87 million.

summary: Warsaw, on the Vistula, was founded about 1300 and became the capital of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1596. After the partitions it became the capital of independent Poland in 1918, and the Second World War destroyed about 85% of it before the Old Town was rebuilt.
notes: START: both articles say the city was established about 1300 by Bolesław II of Masovia; the history article says the new settlement followed Jazdów's raid in 1281 and the Warsaw article gives 'about 1300'. I used 1300 with circa true.

The history article credits Konrad II with a brick church of St John that became the cathedral; the Warsaw article gives the completion of St John's Cathedral as 1390. I give only 1390 for the cathedral and left out the brick church.

Jazdów: the history article says it was founded before 1250 and raided by Lithuanians in 1262 and by Bolesław II in 1281; the Warsaw article says only that it was raided by nearby clans and dukes. I used the history article's account.

Warsaw Uprising deaths: the history article gives c. 170,000 dead (16,000 insurgents) and the Warsaw article gives 150,000 to 200,000 civilian deaths. I used only the 150,000-200,000 range and left out the 170,000.
Dates of German entry in 1915: the history article gives 1 August, the Warsaw article 4 August. I wrote 'summer of 1915'.
Population 1939: the history article gives 1,300,000 and 420,000 in 1945; the Warsaw article has 1 million in 1921 and 1925 in the other. Not contradictory.
Mermaid Sawa and the fisherman Wars are given as folk etymology, as the article states.
Left out as not city history in the sense of the brief: tourism, airports, sports clubs, metro, skyscrapers, the 2022 refugees and the present economic boom.

1794: the article gives 3 November for the Russians reaching the outskirts and four hours of fighting; no separate date is given for the storming, so none is written. Death toll 'up to 20,000' is the article's estimate.

Piłsudski: the history article says he came to the Warsaw-Vienna station on 10 November and received military authority on 11 November; the Warsaw article says he returned on 11 November. I wrote 10 November for his return and 11 November for the authority, as the history article gives them; the editor may check.
Population 1754 (24,000) and 1792 (115,000) are from the history article.
